publicationStmt.publisher: eLiebermann: A Database of Early English Laws and Legal Language, after Felix Liebermann

revisionDesc.change: First draft: general principles, the Legal Dictionary (abbreviations and technical terms, works cited, cross-reference and spelling entries, other dictionaries) and the Lawcodes Database.

div.head: Editorial Principles
div.p: This page records the editorial decisions taken in the making of eLiebermann. It is revised as the work proceeds.

div.head: General
Aims and scope
div.p: eLiebermann has been built from spreadsheets and transcriptions compiled over many years for the editor's own research on the language and composition of the early English laws, and its structure, its corrections and its indexing reflect the questions that research has asked of the texts. It is offered here in the hope that it may be of wider use to others working on the laws, their language and their transmission.

The Lawcodes Database is concerned principally with the Old English laws issued before 1066, together with certain of the other legal texts that Liebermann prints with them. Some post-Conquest codes and compilations have also been included. The Legal Dictionary is an edition of the whole of Liebermann's Wörterbuch.
div.head: Liebermann and beyond
div.p: The project takes its name from Felix Liebermann, and his Gesetze der Angelsachsen is its foundation: his texts, his German translation, his apparatus and his clause divisions are the frame to which everything else is fitted. eLiebermann is, however, more than a digital reproduction of the Gesetze. It gathers beside Liebermann's text the editions and translations of later scholars where these can be reproduced; it organises and corrects the texts, checking them against the printed volumes and against Liebermann's own textual notes and corrections; it records cross-references between clauses drawn from Liebermann's margins and from the scholarship of the following century; and it adds a subject index of the laws that is the editor's own. Where the site departs from or adds to Liebermann, this is noted.
div.head: The base text and its citation
div.p: Liebermann's text is reproduced as he printed it, with his sigla, his numbering and his typography. Readers who wish to verify a reading are referred to the scans of the printed volumes linked from every dictionary entry and clause page. The edition is cited as: Felix Liebermann, ed. and trans., Die Gesetze der Angelsachsen, 3 vols (Halle: Niemeyer, 1903–16).

div.head: The Legal Dictionary
Abbreviations, technical terms and conventional signs
div.p: Liebermann's Wörterbuch relies on a dense system of abbreviations, grammatical terms and conventional signs, which Liebermann nowhere sets out in full. The list of Grammatical Terms and Abbreviations, and the pop-ups drawn from it throughout the dictionary, are the editor's reconstruction of that system. Each item gives (i) the German form as Liebermann wrote it out, or as he would have written it out; (ii) the modern standard German equivalent, where the spelling or the word itself has since changed; and (iii) an English translation; with notes where needed.

Where Liebermann gives no expansion, the meaning has been inferred from his usage. Every one of the c. 500 abbreviations (639 forms in all) has been checked against its occurrences across the entries. The meaning of an exclamation mark after a quoted form, for example, which Liebermann does not explain, is taken as sic on the basis of its appearance where an unexpected or incorrect form appears in a manuscript (e.g. accusative ending where dative might be expected).

Liebermann is not wholly consistent in either his terminology or his abbreviations. One term may appear in more than one abbreviated form, and one abbreviation may serve for more than one term: sbj stands for "subject" in the grammatical notes but for "subjunctive" in the Old French entries. Some expansions offered here are therefore necessarily provisional. The list is meant as an aid to Liebermann's technical and explanatory vocabulary, not as a glossary of the ordinary German of his definitions, whose words are accordingly not linked. Corrections are welcome through Make a suggestion.
div.head: Authors and works cited
div.p: Liebermann prints no bibliography, and cites modern scholarship and editions by short title. The full citations on the list of Authors and Works Cited have been reconstructed by the editor from those short titles, from the two brief lists of works in the Gesetze (I, p. LIV; II.2, p. 262), and from the editions current when he wrote. Where Liebermann cites a primary source without naming an edition, the edition he most probably used is given. These identifications are marked as provisional until they can be checked against the relevant editions.
div.head: Cross-reference and spelling entries
div.p: Each entry that serves only to send the reader to another headword is shown with the headword(s) to which it refers, without the further apparatus of a full entry. Headwords that record a spelling rather than a word (for example aa for ā) are marked as spelling entries.
div.head: Other dictionaries
div.p: Headwords are linked to the corresponding entries in the Bosworth–Toller Anglo-Saxon Dictionary. These links are added by the project team, and are a work in progress.

div.head: The Lawcodes Database
Clause division
div.p: Liebermann's division of the laws into clauses is followed throughout, so that every citation of the form used by Liebermann and by the scholarship that depends on him leads to a single clause. The texts of later editions are divided at Liebermann's clause breaks, including those printed by their editors as continuous prose. Where a later editor divides a clause more finely, the clause is kept whole and the editor's divisions are marked within it by that editor's own numbers.
div.head: Manuscripts
div.p: Every text is identified by the manuscript from which it is taken, under Liebermann's siglum. Where Liebermann offers the text from more than one manuscript, his main text (taken to be that in the leftmost column) is given first.
div.head: Translations
div.p: Liebermann's German translation is accompanied by a close, semi-literal English rendering, made with the assistance of a large language model and so labelled. This is intended as a crib to Liebermann's German, and so to his understanding of the law; it is not a new translation of the Old English, and should not be quoted as one. The translations of modern editors follow, each attributed.
div.head: Liebermann's notes
div.p: Liebermann's textual notes and his commentary (the Erklärungen of volume III) are given in his German as printed, with an English rendering, and are hidden by default, to be shown clause by clause. Much of this commentary, and the legal comparisons drawn by Liebermann, has been superseded by later scholarship; it is included as part of the record of Liebermann's edition.
div.head: Cross-references between clauses
div.p: The Early English legal corpus contains many laws that repeat or draw upon earlier laws; certain "early" laws are in fact historical forgeries composed by later writers. A database recording similarities between clauses offers a useful means of tracing these quirks of legislative composition. Accordingly, Liebermann's marginal cross-references and points of similarity or comparison made by later scholars are given with their source and page, and are linked in both directions. The wording on each clause page distinguishes the references made at that clause from those made at other clauses that point to it. Suggestions for additional links are welcome.
div.head: Subject index
div.p: Every clause has been read and indexed by the offences, people, places and other matters with which it deals. The index was created for this project, and is independent of Liebermann's Rechts- und Sachglossar.
